title: Capstone: Knowledge Graphs
blurb: Tests why a capstone on a new domain is stronger evidence than a re-run, validating extraction on new data, reusing traversal code unmodified as a generalisation test, the unanswerable-question check, and how to compare two benchmarks by shape rather than by number.

§83.2.2 The Traversal Function Needed Zero Changes

questions.prompt: Why does the capstone build a new domain instead of re-running Chapter 82's pipeline?
options: To test a new traversal algorithm
To check the result isn't a dataset artefact
To get higher precision than Chapter 82 reported
Because the procurement graph was too large to reuse
questions.explanation: Every earlier chapter used the same procurement graph. Reproducing the pattern on new data is stronger evidence than a good result on familiar data.

questions.prompt: What counts as success when the capstone's numbers differ from Chapter 82's?
options: GraphRAG wins by the same margin on both graphs.
Vector-RAG scores zero on every question.
The precision and recall values match to three decimals.
The same shape of result appears on the new graph.
questions.explanation: Different graph, questions and gold labels give different numbers. The claim holds if the pattern holds.

questions.prompt: Why did extraction validation matter more here than in Chapter 78?
options: The new graph had more edges than Chapter 78's.
Chapter 78 skipped validation entirely.
The passages were written by an LLM.
The extraction was never tuned on this data.
questions.explanation: If extraction only worked by accident on familiar examples, unsupported edges would show up here. Each edge was traced to its source passage.

refLinks.label: §83.2.1 Extraction Had to Be Genuinely Validated, Not Assumed

questions.prompt: The capstone graph has 7 authors and 6 papers. How many nodes does it have?
questions.explanation: 7 + 6 = 13 nodes, joined by 15 validated AUTHORED_BY and CITES edges built from 12 passages.

questions.prompt: What did reusing agentic_search unmodified on CITES edges show?
options: The traversal must be rewritten for every new relation type.
The traversal was never specific to ownership hierarchies.
The function only works on graphs with 13 nodes.
Citation graphs need deeper hop budgets than ownership graphs.
questions.explanation: Same code, new relation, new graph, zero changes. The logic was more general than its first chapter's framing.

refLinks.label: §83.2.2 The Traversal Function Needed Zero Changes

questions.prompt: In the capstone's unanswerable question, what did citation_chain_search do?
options: It returned the closest paper by text similarity.
It returned a chain through an author node.
It looped until max_hops ran out with an error.
It stopped at the start and reported no match.
questions.explanation: The starting paper had no outgoing CITES edges, so no chain existed. The search didn't invent one.

refLinks.label: §83.2.3 The “No Valid Answer” Case Reappeared, Independently

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 83.3 call the unanswerable question a more important check than any answerable one?
options: It is the easiest question for both methods.
It shows which method is faster.
It raises the average precision of both methods.
It catches methods that fabricate answers.
questions.explanation: Answerable questions test finding. Only an unanswerable one tests honest failure.

questions.prompt: How did single-hop results differ between Chapter 82 and the capstone?
options: Both graphs showed an exact tie.
A tie, then a modest GraphRAG edge
Vector-RAG won on the citation graph.
GraphRAG lost on both graphs.
questions.explanation: Capstone single-hop precision was 0.167 for vector-RAG and 0.350 for GraphRAG. GraphRAG was at least as good on both graphs.

questions.prompt: Which statements match the capstone's multi-hop results? Select all that apply.
options: GraphRAG precision was 0.800 against vector-RAG's 0.343.
GraphRAG recall was 1.000.
The two methods tied on precision.
GraphRAG was ahead on both precision and recall.
Vector-RAG recall was higher than GraphRAG's.
questions.explanation: Vector-RAG reached 0.750 recall and 0.343 precision. GraphRAG led on both metrics, as on the procurement graph.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter say about its 6-question benchmark?
options: It proves GraphRAG wins on any citation graph.
It shows the method, not a statistical claim.
It is large enough for a production decision.
It is too small to show any pattern at all.
questions.explanation: A production decision should run the same by-type scoring over dozens to hundreds of questions from real usage.

questions.prompt: Your team gets a strong GraphRAG result on its own procurement graph and wants to roll it out to legal documents. What does the capstone suggest first?
options: Ship it, since the result already reproduced once.
Score the pipeline on legal data by type.
Drop vector-RAG, since GraphRAG won.
Rewrite the traversal for legal relation types first.
questions.explanation: Results hold per domain only once measured there. The traversal may well reuse unmodified, and single-hop questions may still suit vector-RAG.

bookExercises.prompt: State this capstone's core methodological claim ("reproducing the same shape of result on new data is stronger evidence than...") in your own words.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A good result reproduced on a completely different dataset, using the same methodology, is stronger evidence the underlying claim is a real property of the methods being tested, rather than an artefact of one specific dataset's quirks that happened to produce a favourable-looking number.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three specific prior-chapter techniques this capstone reuses (extraction-with-validation, adaptive traversal, precision/recall-by-type evaluation) and state which one required zero code changes to work on the new domain.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Extraction-with-validation discipline (Chapter 78), adaptive traversal (Chapter 81), precision/recall-by-type evaluation (Chapter 82). The adaptive traversal function required zero code changes to work on the new domain: the exact same `agentic_search` code, applied to a `CITES` relation instead of `OWNS`, on an entirely different graph.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the comparison table (Chapter 82's exact single-hop tie vs. this capstone's modest GraphRAG single-hop edge), explain why these two DIFFERENT specific numbers are still consistent with, rather than contradicting, the underlying claim that GraphRAG helps most on multi-hop questions.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The two results are consistent, not contradictory, because the claim being tested is about the *shape* of the pattern (GraphRAG ties or modestly beats vector-RAG on single-hop, substantially beats it on multi-hop) rather than about any specific numeric value being reproduced exactly. An exact tie on one graph and a modest edge on a different graph both fall within "GraphRAG is at least as good as vector-RAG on single-hop questions." The qualitative claim holds in both cases even though the precise numbers differ, which is exactly what would be expected if the effect is real and generalizes, since different graphs and different specific questions would naturally produce somewhat different exact values even under a consistently true underlying pattern.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the unanswerable-question result (the citation-chain search correctly stopping rather than fabricating a match), explain why this specific check, reappearing independently on new data, is stronger evidence of good benchmark-design habits than if the exact same unanswerable question had simply been copied from Chapter 82's benchmark.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: An unanswerable-question check that emerges independently (designed fresh for a new domain without reference to the earlier chapters' specific question) is stronger evidence of a generally good benchmark-design habit than reusing the identical question would be, because independent re-derivation shows the practice ("always include a no-valid-answer case") was internalized as a principle rather than mechanically copied. If the exact same question had simply been copied over, it would only show the specific test case transferred, not that the underlying design discipline generalizes to genuinely new benchmark construction. The independent reappearance is evidence about the *methodology*, not just about one recurring test case.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague argues "we already validated GraphRAG's advantage in the earlier chapters; building a whole second benchmark on a new domain for the capstone is redundant busywork." Using this chapter's Motivation and Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "The earlier chapters validated GraphRAG's advantage on one specific graph, built and tuned by the same person who wrote the extraction and retrieval code. That's exactly the scenario where a pipeline could quietly work only because it was (even unintentionally) shaped around that one example's quirks. Building a second benchmark on genuinely new data, with a different domain's entities, relations, and question shapes, is the only way to distinguish 'this technique generally works' from 'this technique works on the example we happened to build it against.' That's not redundant, it's the entire point of a capstone."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 83.2 treats reusing prior code unmodified as a generalisation test. Describe what it would have meant, as a finding, if `citation_chain_search` had required code changes to work on the new citation graph. What would that have revealed about Chapter 81's original traversal function?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If `citation_chain_search` had required code changes to work on the new citation graph, that would have revealed the original Chapter 81 traversal function was more specific to ownership-hierarchy graphs than its general framing suggested. Perhaps it implicitly assumed something about the `OWNS` relation's structure (e.g., a tree-like hierarchy without cycles, or a specific directionality convention) that doesn't hold for `CITES` relationships, meaning the "general BFS traversal" claim would have been narrower in practice than in name, and the capstone would have surfaced a real limitation worth documenting rather than confirming a clean generalisation.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Book 2's capstone chapter's scoping discipline once more, alongside this capstone's own structure. Identify one specific way this knowledge-graphs capstone follows that discipline (every stage gets a real, if modest, version) and one way it differs in emphasis given its specific goal of testing generalisation rather than exercising the full data-science lifecycle.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: This capstone follows Book 2's "every stage gets a real, if modest, version" discipline directly: extraction, graph construction, both retrieval strategies, and evaluation are all present and genuinely measured on the new domain, rather than one stage (e.g. extraction) being done impressively while others are skipped or faked. Where it differs in emphasis: Book 2's capstone chapter is about exercising the FULL data-science lifecycle end to end (problem framing through deployment and monitoring) on a novel problem chosen by the practitioner, while this knowledge-graphs capstone has a narrower, more specific goal: reusing an already-designed pipeline's exact components on a deliberately different domain, specifically to test whether the earlier chapters' findings generalise, rather than demonstrating the practitioner's ability to scope and sequence an entirely open-ended project from scratch.
